passages.t: The women who travelled with Jesus
passages.happening:
Soon afterward Jesus travels from town to town and village to village, preaching the good news of the kingdom of God. The twelve are with him.

So are some women who had been healed of evil spirits and illnesses. Luke names three: “Mary called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out” (verse 2); “Joanna the wife of Herod's household manager Chuza” (verse 3); and Susanna. There are many others too. “These women were ministering to them out of their own means” (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
Only Luke tells us this. Mark mentions women who had followed Jesus and cared for him in Galilee, but only when they stand watching at the cross (Mark 15:40-41). Luke names them early, while the work in Galilee is going on, and tells us they paid for it.

‘Ministering to them out of their own means’ means they supported Jesus and the twelve with their own money and goods. This is the only place in the Gospels that says plainly how Jesus' travelling work was paid for. A group of men on the road for months needed food and shelter, and these women provided it.

Mary called Magdalene was most likely from Magdala, a fishing town on the western shore of the lake. In 2009 archaeologists found there a synagogue from before AD 70, built and used in the time of Jesus. Early Christians remembered Magdala as her home town.

Joanna's husband Chuza managed the household and estates of Herod Antipas, the ruler of Galilee. That was a senior post at court. So the news about Jesus had reached the household of the man who had put John the Baptist in prison. Joanna appears again at the empty tomb (24:10). Susanna is not mentioned anywhere else. All we know of her is her name and her gift.

How unusual was it for women to travel with a teacher and pay his way? We cannot say exactly, and Luke does not stop to explain. But he clearly wants these women remembered by name. The site's guide on women in the ancient world tells more about the world they lived in.
passages.ot:
In the Old Testament, women who gave from what they had to support God's servants were remembered. A widow at Zarephath fed Elijah from her last flour and oil (1 Kings 17:15), and Luke has already reminded his readers of her (4:26). A well-to-do woman of Shunem fed Elisha whenever he passed by, and made a room for him (2 Kings 4:8-10).

The prophet Joel promised a day when God would pour out his Spirit “on all people” and “your sons and daughters will prophesy” (Joel 2:28). In Acts, Luke shows that day coming (Acts 2:17-18).
passages.hard:
Was Mary Magdalene a prostitute? The Gospels never say so. Luke says seven demons had gone out of her. That tells us she had suffered greatly and been set free. It says nothing about her morals, and Luke never treats being troubled by demons as a sexual sin. The idea that she was a reformed prostitute came much later. In a sermon preached in 591, Pope Gregory the Great joined her with Mary of Bethany and with the unnamed ‘sinful woman’ of the chapter before (7:36-50), who is not called a prostitute either. In the Western church that picture stuck for centuries. The Eastern churches kept the women apart. Luke introduces Mary here as someone new, right after that story, with no hint that she is the same woman.

What the Gospels do say about Mary Magdalene is remarkable. She followed Jesus from Galilee, gave from what she had, stood near the cross, and was one of the first to hear that he had risen (24:10).
passages.asks: These women gave out of what they had, and their names are in the Bible because of it. Your help to God's work may feel small or unseen, but it is not unseen to him. Ask what you have, money, time, a home, a skill, that could support the work of the gospel. And if your past has been told about you wrongly, notice how the church got Mary wrong, and how Jesus never did.

passages.happening:
A large crowd is gathering from town after town, and Jesus tells a parable. A farmer goes out to sow. Some seed falls on the path, where it is trampled and the birds eat it. Some falls on rock; it comes up but withers, because it has no moisture. Some falls among thorns, which grow up with it and choke it. Some falls on good soil and grows, and produces a crop a hundred times what was sown. Then he calls out, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (verse 8).

His disciples ask what the parable means. He says that the secrets of the kingdom have been given to them, but to others he speaks in parables, so that ‘though seeing, they may not see; though hearing, they may not understand.’

Then he explains: “The seed is the word of God” (verse 11). The path is those who hear, but the devil takes the word away. The rock is those who receive it with joy but have no root; “They believe for a season, but in the time of testing, they fall away” (verse 13). The thorns are those choked by the worries, riches and pleasures of life. The good soil is “those with a noble and good heart, who hear the word, cling to it, and by persevering produce a crop” (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
Mark and Matthew tell this parable too (Mark 4:1-20; Matthew 13:1-23), and their notes explain the farming. A farmer scattered seed by hand. Paths ran through and beside the fields, in places rock lay just under a thin skin of earth, and thorns grew everywhere.

Luke tells it a little differently. He says plainly, ‘The seed is the word of God’. He says the rocky ground had ‘no moisture’. He speaks of believing ‘for a season’ and falling away ‘in the time of testing’, where Mark has trouble and persecution. He names ‘pleasures’ along with worries and riches as the thorns. And he describes the good soil as ‘a noble and good heart’.

Above all, Luke adds ‘by persevering’. Good soil is not only a heart that receives the word with joy on the first day. It is a heart that holds on, through dry seasons and thorns, until the crop comes.

Luke has just told of women who used their own means for Jesus (verses 1-3). Now he warns that riches can choke the word. Money can serve the kingdom or strangle it.
passages.ot:
The words about seeing and not seeing come from Isaiah 6. When God sent Isaiah, he warned that the people would “Be ever hearing, but never understanding; be ever seeing, but never perceiving” (Isaiah 6:9). Isaiah's message would harden those who had already turned away.

God's word in Isaiah is also pictured as rain and seed: “so My word that proceeds from My mouth will not return to Me empty” (Isaiah 55:11). However much seed is lost, the harvest comes.
passages.hard:
Does Jesus tell parables so that people will not understand? On its plainest reading, verse 10 can sound that way, and readers have felt the difficulty from the start. Luke shortens the saying and leaves out the line about being forgiven that Mark has.

Christians have answered in different ways. Some read the words as God's judgment on people who had already refused him: the truth hidden in the story becomes a hardening for those who will not come near. Many add that in Isaiah the words describe a people who had already hardened themselves. Others stress that a parable invites the listener in: those who ask, as the disciples did, are given the meaning. Luke's next verses point that way: a lamp is meant to be seen, and nothing hidden will stay hidden (verses 16-17). Christians who stress God's choosing and those who stress human freedom have read this verse differently for centuries. Both agree on what the chapter keeps saying: listen.
passages.asks: Which soil are you today? Most people have known all four at different times. Ask what is choking the word in you: worry, money, or pleasure. And notice the word Luke adds: persevering. Faith that lasts is not a burst of joy, but a steady holding on.

passages.happening:
“No one lights a lamp and covers it with a jar or puts it under a bed. Instead, he sets it on a stand, so those who enter can see the light” (verse 16).

Nothing hidden will stay hidden. Nothing secret will stay unknown. “Pay attention, therefore, to how you listen” (verse 18). Whoever has will be given more. Whoever does not have will lose even what he thinks he has.
passages.hearers:
Mark has these sayings too (Mark 4:21-25), and its notes explain the lamp. A house lamp was a small clay dish of olive oil with a wick, and a village home might have only one. Hiding it would be silly.

Luke places these sayings right after the sower, and they belong with it. The word of God is a light. It is meant to be seen, not hidden. And it is heard well or badly.

‘Take care how you listen’ is the hinge. Those who listen and keep what they hear are given more understanding. Those who hear and let it go will find that even what they thought they had slips away.

Luke adds ‘so those who enter can see the light’. A lamp on a stand helps the people coming in from outside. The light of the gospel is not only for those already in the house.
passages.ot: The psalm says, “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path” (Psalm 119:105). Israel was to be “a light for the nations” (Isaiah 49:6), and Simeon called the child Jesus “a light for revelation to the Gentiles” (2:32).
passages.hard: ‘Whoever does not have, even what he thinks he has will be taken away’ sounds unfair. But Jesus is speaking about listening, not money. Truth that is heard and ignored does not stay put. It fades. Truth that is heard and acted on grows. The saying is a warning to pay attention, not a rule about wealth.
passages.asks: Jesus does not only say ‘listen’. He says ‘pay attention to how you listen’. When you read the Bible or hear it taught, do you listen to argue, to collect facts, or to obey? Who could see the light more clearly if your faith were on a stand instead of under a jar?

passages.happening:
Jesus' mother and brothers come to see him, but they cannot reach him because of the crowd. Someone tells him, “Your mother and brothers are standing outside, wanting to see You” (verse 20).

He answers, “My mother and brothers are those who hear the word of God and carry it out” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
Mark and Matthew tell this too (Mark 3:31-35; Matthew 12:46-50). In Mark the scene follows the family's worry that Jesus is ‘out of his mind’ (Mark 3:21), and it can sound sharp. Luke tells it more gently. He leaves out the family's worry and puts the saying right after the sower and the lamp. ‘Hear the word of God and carry it out’ is the good soil of verse 15.

Luke has already shown Jesus' mother as the first to hear God's word and keep it. She said, “May it happen to me according to your word” (1:38), and she treasured up all these things in her heart (2:19). So the saying does not push Mary aside. It shows why she belongs to him twice over: by birth, and by hearing and doing.

Who were Jesus' brothers? Christians have understood this in different ways. Many Protestants take them as children born to Mary and Joseph after Jesus. The Orthodox tradition has often taken them as Joseph's children from an earlier marriage, and the Roman Catholic tradition as cousins or close relatives. The Greek word for brother can be used for close kin. This is a question on which faithful Christians differ.
passages.ot:
Moses said God would raise up a prophet, and “You must listen to him” (Deuteronomy 18:15). Hearing and doing is the heart of the law. Moses told Israel to hear God's statutes, and to “Learn them and observe them carefully” (Deuteronomy 5:1).

The psalm promises that God takes in those who have lost family: “Though my father and mother forsake me, the LORD will receive me” (Psalm 27:10).
passages.hard: Is Jesus rejecting his family? No. Luke gives no sign of a quarrel. Jesus is widening the family, not leaving it. Later, from the cross in John's Gospel, he makes sure his mother is cared for (John 19:26-27). Belonging to Jesus' family does not cancel love for your own. But it means that no one is left without a family who hears and does God's word.
passages.asks: Jesus says his family is made of people who hear God's word and do it. If you have lost family, or feel like an outsider in your own, you can belong here. And if you have a family in the church, ask whether you treat its members like brothers and sisters, or like strangers you sit near.

passages.happening:
One day Jesus says, “Let us cross to the other side of the lake” (verse 22). They set out, and he falls asleep. A windstorm comes down on the lake. The boat is filling with water, and they are in great danger.

The disciples wake him: “Master, Master, we are perishing!” (verse 24). He gets up and rebukes the wind and the raging water, and they stop. All is calm.

“Where is your faith?” he asks them (verse 25). Frightened and amazed, they ask one another, “Who is this? He commands even the winds and the water, and they obey Him!” (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
Mark and Matthew tell this story too (Mark 4:35-41; Matthew 8:23-27), and their notes explain the lake. It lies far below sea level in a bowl ringed by hills, and cool air can pour down from the heights and stir up sudden, violent storms. Several of these men were fishermen who knew the lake well. If they thought they would drown, the storm was real.

Luke tells it briefly, and with gentler words for the disciples. In Mark they say, “don't You care that we are perishing?” (Mark 4:38), and Jesus asks, ‘Do you still have no faith?’ In Luke they cry, ‘Master, Master’, and Jesus asks, ‘Where is your faith?’ They have faith. They have just lost hold of it in the storm.

Jesus ‘rebukes’ the wind, the same word Luke used for the demon and the fever (4:35, 39). Luke treats the storm, like sickness and evil, as something that must obey him.
passages.ot:
In the Old Testament, only God rules the sea. “You rule the raging sea; when its waves mount up, You still them” (Psalm 89:9). The psalm tells of sailors in a storm who cried to the LORD, and “He calmed the storm to a whisper, and the waves of the sea were hushed” (Psalm 107:29). The disciples' question, ‘Who is this?’, has an answer in their own Scriptures.

Jonah, too, slept in a boat in a storm (Jonah 1:4-5). But Jonah was running from God. Jesus sleeps because he trusts his Father, and then he stills the storm himself.
passages.hard: Does ‘Where is your faith?’ mean that frightened people are failing God? No. The disciples did the right thing: they turned to Jesus. His question is not a sneer. It invites them to remember who is in the boat with them. Fear in a storm is human, and being afraid is not the same as having no faith. If anxiety is a storm you live with, getting help from a doctor or counsellor is wise, and not a lack of faith.
passages.asks: Jesus did not promise there would be no storms. He was in the boat when the storm came. What storm are you in? Where is your faith in it: in your own strength, in the boat, or in the one who is with you? The disciples ended with a question, ‘Who is this?’ Ask it too, and follow it to its answer.

passages.happening:
They land in the region of the Gerasenes, across the lake from Galilee. A man from the town meets Jesus. He is possessed by demons. For a long time he has worn no clothes and lived not in a house but among the tombs.

When he sees Jesus he cries out and falls down before him: “What do You want with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg You not to torture me!” (verse 28). Jesus had already ordered the unclean spirit to come out. It had often seized him; he had been kept in chains and shackles, but he broke them and was driven into lonely places.

“What is your name?” Jesus asks. “Legion,” he replies, because many demons had gone into him (verse 30). They beg Jesus not to send them into the Abyss. A large herd of pigs is feeding on the hillside, and the demons beg to go into them. Jesus lets them. The herd rushes down the steep bank into the lake and drowns.

The herdsmen run and tell everyone. People come out and find the man “sitting at Jesus' feet, clothed and in his right mind; and they were afraid” (verse 35). The whole region asks Jesus to leave. The man begs to go with him, but Jesus sends him home: “Return home and describe how much God has done for you” (verse 39). The man goes through the whole town telling how much Jesus has done for him.
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this story at greater length (Mark 5:1-20), and Matthew tells of two men (Matthew 8:28-34). Their notes explain the setting. For a Jewish hearer, every detail says ‘unclean’: Gentile country on the east side of the lake, a man with an unclean spirit, living among graves, beside a herd of pigs. The law called the pig unclean (Leviticus 11:7), and touching a grave made a person unclean. Jesus walks straight into the middle of it.

The name Legion would have struck hard. A legion was a unit of the Roman army, some five thousand soldiers. The man is held by something like an army.

The place is a puzzle. Old copies of the Gospels read Gerasenes, Gadarenes, or Gergesenes. The city of Gerasa lay some thirty miles from the lake. In the 200s the scholar Origen pointed to a town called Gergesa on the shore. At Kursi, on the east shore, a steep slope and the ruins of a large monastery were uncovered in the 1970s, and many think this was the place, though not all agree.

Only Luke mentions the Abyss, a word for the deep prison of evil powers (Revelation 20:3). The spirits fear being shut away for good.

Luke's picture of the healed man is careful. He is ‘sitting at Jesus' feet’, the place of a student with a teacher. Mary of Bethany will sit there too (10:39), and Paul says he was trained ‘at the feet of’ his teacher Gamaliel (Acts 22:3). The wild man is now a disciple.

Notice the wording at the end. Jesus tells him to tell what ‘God’ has done. He goes and tells what ‘Jesus’ has done. Luke lets the reader notice that the two are spoken of as one.
passages.ot:
Isaiah once described a rebellious people “sitting among the graves” and “eating the meat of pigs” (Isaiah 65:4). The scene here is like that picture come to life, and Jesus comes into it to set a man free.

The psalm says, “God settles the lonely in families; He leads the prisoners out” (Psalm 68:6). The man who lived alone among the dead is sent home to his people.
passages.hard:
Was this man possessed by spirits, or was he mentally ill, described in the language of his time? Luke presents a real spiritual power that speaks, bargains, and leaves. Many modern readers think of illness instead. Christians have answered in more than one way. Many hold that both are real: that most suffering of the mind is illness, to be met with medicine and care, and that the Bible also speaks of evil powers that are more than illness. Most warn strongly against treating every illness as a demon. Luke's point is not to give a diagnosis. It is that nothing that holds a person, however strong, is stronger than Jesus.

Mark adds that the man was harming himself (Mark 5:5). If that is where you or someone you love is today, please reach out for real help now, to a doctor, a pastor, or a crisis line.

Why did Jesus let the spirits destroy the herd, and the owners' living with it? Luke does not say, and it is wise not to claim too much. Some point out that Jesus only gave permission and that the destruction was the spirits' own work, showing what they had meant to do to the man. Others say the drowned herd was visible proof that the spirits were truly gone. Others see a sign that one human life is worth more than a herd. It is honest to admit that the passage does not answer every question it raises.
passages.asks: The townspeople were more afraid of the calm man than of the wild one, and they asked Jesus to leave. Is there any part of your life where you have quietly asked Jesus to stay away because his coming would cost you something? And notice the healed man's first task: to go home and tell the people who knew him at his worst what God had done.

passages.t: A woman who touched his cloak
passages.happening:
When Jesus returns, the crowd welcomes him. A synagogue leader named Jairus falls at his feet and begs him to come to his house, because his only daughter, about twelve years old, is dying. As Jesus goes, the crowds press around him.

In the crowd is a woman who has suffered from bleeding for twelve years. No one has been able to heal her. She comes up behind Jesus and touches the fringe of his cloak, and at once her bleeding stops.

“Who touched Me?” Jesus asks (verse 45). Everyone denies it, and Peter points out that the whole crowd is pressing against him. But Jesus says, “Someone touched Me, for I know that power has gone out from Me” (verse 46).

The woman sees that she cannot hide. Trembling, she falls down before him and tells, in front of everyone, why she touched him and how she was healed at once. “Daughter,” says Jesus, “your faith has healed you. Go in peace” (verse 48).
passages.hearers:
Mark and Matthew tell this story too (Mark 5:21-34; Matthew 9:18-22), and their notes explain it. Under the law of Moses, a woman with a long flow of blood was ritually unclean for as long as it lasted (Leviticus 15:25). ‘Unclean’ here does not mean sinful or dirty. It meant she could not come near to worship at the temple, and people who touched her things had to wash. Scholars debate how cut off from daily life this made her. But twelve years of illness would have worn down anyone.

The fringe of the cloak was probably one of the tassels the law told Israelites to wear on the corners of their clothes (Numbers 15:38).

Mark says she had spent all she had on doctors, and only grown worse (Mark 5:26). Luke says simply that no one could heal her. Some old copies of Luke also say she had spent all she had on doctors; others, among the oldest, leave that out.

Luke tells us she spoke ‘in the presence of all the people’. A woman who had lived on the edge for twelve years is now at the centre, telling her story, and Jesus calls her ‘Daughter’.
passages.ot: By the law's rules, her touch should have made Jesus unclean (Leviticus 15:19-27). Instead the flow goes the other way. His power makes her well. Isaiah spoke of the servant of God who “took on our infirmities and carried our sorrows” (Isaiah 53:4), and Matthew applies those words to Jesus' healings (Matthew 8:17).
passages.hard:
Why did Jesus make her come forward? She was already healed, and she was afraid. It can look harsh. But if she had slipped away, she would have had her body healed and nothing more. By calling her out, Jesus lets the crowd see that she is clean. He gives her his word of peace, not just his power. And he names what happened: it was not magic in his cloak but her trust in him that he honours.

‘Your faith has healed you’ does not mean that those who are not healed lacked faith. The note on Luke 5:12-16 says plainly what the Bible does and does not teach about sickness and faith.
passages.asks: She came hoping to get help without being seen. Jesus wanted more for her than that. Ask whether you come to God hoping for help while keeping your distance. What would it mean to come forward and tell him the whole truth, and to hear him call you ‘Daughter’ or ‘Son’?

passages.happening:
While Jesus is still speaking, someone comes from Jairus's house. “Your daughter is dead,” he tells Jairus. “Do not bother the Teacher anymore” (verse 49).

Jesus hears it and says to Jairus, “Do not be afraid; just believe, and she will be healed” (verse 50).

At the house he lets no one go in with him except Peter, John and James, and the girl's father and mother. Everyone is weeping and mourning for her. Jesus says, “Stop weeping; she is not dead but asleep” (verse 52). They laugh at him, knowing she is dead.

He takes her by the hand and calls out, “Child, get up!” (verse 54). Her spirit returns, and at once she gets up. He tells them to give her something to eat. Her parents are astounded, but Jesus orders them not to tell anyone what has happened.
passages.hearers:
Mark and Matthew tell this too (Mark 5:35-43; Matthew 9:23-26), and their notes explain the mourners. Mourning began at once when someone died. Families hired flute players and women who wailed. A rule recorded in the Mishnah, written down around AD 200, says that even a poor man must provide at least two flute players and one wailing woman for his wife's funeral.

The two stories are told together on purpose. While Jesus stopped for the woman, the girl died. Both are called ‘daughter’. The woman had been ill for twelve years. The girl was about twelve years old.

Luke notices that this was an only child, as he did with the widow's son at Nain (7:12), and as he will with a boy in the next chapter (9:38).

Mark keeps Jesus' Aramaic words, ‘Talitha koum’. Luke gives them in Greek for his readers: “Child, get up!” (verse 54). Only Luke says ‘her spirit returned’. He wants it clear that she had truly died and truly came back.

Jesus thinks of something everyone else has forgotten. A girl who has been ill needs to eat.
passages.ot: The words ‘her spirit returned’ recall Elijah, who prayed over a widow's son, “O LORD my God, please let this boy's life return to him!” (1 Kings 17:21), and the boy lived. Daniel spoke of those who “sleep in the dust of the earth” who will awake (Daniel 12:2). Jesus calls death ‘sleep’ because, for him, it is something a person can be woken from.
passages.hard:
Jesus says the girl is “not dead but asleep” (verse 52). Was she only in a coma? Luke does not mean that. The messenger says she is dead, the mourners are sure of it, and Luke says her spirit returned. Calling death ‘sleep’ was a way of speaking about death from God's side.

This story, like the one at Nain, does not promise that every child who dies will be given back now. If you have lost a child, or someone you love, it does not say they were loved less than Jairus's daughter. It shows who Jesus is, and the hope of the day when he will wake all who sleep. If grief is crushing you, do not carry it alone. Reach out to people you trust, to a pastor, or to someone trained to help.
passages.asks: Between the bad news and the miracle, Jesus gives Jairus one sentence: ‘Do not be afraid; just believe.’ Where are you hearing a voice that says ‘Do not bother the Teacher anymore’? Keep walking with Jesus anyway. And notice the last detail: the Lord of life remembers that a hungry girl needs her supper.
